title: The NAND Price Cycle Has Turned and SanDisk Owns the Fallout
subtitle: An 85% gross margin looks like a franchise until spot prices drop 20% in a month.
summary: SanDisk reported historic quarterly profits driven by an AI-fueled memory crunch, but market researchers now project an end to the NAND pricing boom. With contract rates turning negative and supply ramping back up, investors are aggressively discounting the sustainability of peak-cycle margins.

bodyHtml:
SanDisk makes NAND flash memory: the silicon chips that keep your data intact when you turn your machine off. It is the same storage technology packed into your smartphone to hold your photos and inside your laptop. It is also stacked inside the massive solid-state drives that feed data into enterprise AI clusters.

Share prices are restated for the eight-for-one split effective November 19, 2026. Market cap uses yesterday’s close. All other figures as of November 20, 2026.

If high-bandwidth memory acts like an AI model's short-term working memory during a conversation, SanDisk makes the permanent library it reads from before answering. Spun out of Western Digital early last year, the company runs joint-venture fabrication plants in Japan with Kioxia. That makes it a pure, unhedged wager on the market price of digital storage.

By standard accounting metrics, its latest quarter was absurd. SanDisk posted $11 billion in revenue, nearly quintupling sales from a year ago while generating over $8 billion of quarterly net income. Gross margins expanded from under 30% to 85% across four quarters, leaving the company debt-free with more than $5 billion in cash.

But in commodity memory, peak profits rarely mean durable franchises. An 85% gross margin at a flash memory fabricator is not software-like pricing power; it is an auction price in the middle of a temporary panic.

That reality hit the tape hard in midday trading, with SanDisk tumbling roughly 16% as the broader semiconductor sector retreated. Investors glancing at weekly charts might mistake an 87% nominal step-down for an overnight crash, but that is just an eight-for-one forward stock split taking effect.

Adjusting for the split, the stock has halved over the past month. It sits roughly 70% below its June peak, even though it is still up more than 100% this year. Peers like Micron and Western Digital also shed double-digit percentages as the memory complex reassessed how long this shortage can last.

The chill arrived via research house TrendForce, which formally called an end to the historic NAND upcycle. TrendForce warned that blended contract prices will drop 0% to 5% sequentially in the first quarter of next year. Every major product category enters a downcycle by mid-year.

Industry spot prices have already plunged more than 20%, and the firm cut its fourth-quarter forecast for contract price increases from 15-20% to 8-13%. Making matters worse, global bit supply is still set to expand 25% to 30%, funded by nearly $30 billion of fresh industry capital spending. That is added capacity flowing into an engine that is already losing steam.

For SanDisk's equity to stabilize and re-rate higher, two specific mechanics have to hold. First, the first-quarter contract settlement must print flat rather than down 5%. That would prove management's multi-year agreements with cloud giants deflect price declines rather than simply delay them. Second, data-center demand, which surged 61% sequentially to more than 40% of revenue, must keep outpacing the drag from consumer hardware.

Consumer revenue shrank 39% year over year, and device makers are actively trimming the storage capacity inside their hardware to protect their own margins. When volume stops growing while unit prices turn downward, trailing earnings multiples fall into the single digits for a reason.

The short thesis is brutally simple: operating leverage works both ways, and management just bought the top of its own cycle. When spot prices slide 20% ahead of contract negotiations, contract prices tend to follow, and an 85% gross margin can evaporate in a matter of quarters.

TrendForce notes that Chinese cloud providers are cutting enterprise solid-state drive orders faster than American hyperscalers are adding them. That creates an inventory overhang just as suppliers bring 25% to 30% more capacity online. The tell came from the executive suite. SanDisk spent $5 billion last quarter repurchasing its own stock at roughly two and a half times where the equity trades today. If the first-quarter contract benchmark prints at a 5% decline, those trailing earnings will look like a historical artifact rather than a baseline.

Bulls argue this downcycle will look different because the AI buildout operates under stricter contractual terms. SanDisk's leadership says half of this fiscal year's bit output and two-thirds of the following year are committed under take-or-pay structures backed by major cloud customers.

Micron echoed that resilience this week, noting three-quarters of its 2027 supply is already sold out and that its take-or-pay deals carry $32 billion of upfront cash. What we are watching is the first-quarter contract pricing print in early 2027: if realized prices hold firm, the market's fears will look like a mispriced panic. If contract rates crack, the multiple will prove to have been a warning.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in SNDK. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
